paragraphs: Of all the powers proposed to be given to the federal government for creating and directing the national forces, I have met with only one specific objection. If I understand it correctly, it is that proper provision has not been made against standing armies in time of peace. I shall now try to show that this objection rests on weak and unsubstantial foundations.

It has indeed been put forward in the vaguest and most general form, supported only by bold assertions, with no appearance of argument and not even the backing of theoretical opinion. It contradicts the practice of other free nations and the general sense of America, as expressed in most of the existing constitutions. The correctness of this remark will be plain the moment we recall that the objection turns on a supposed need to restrain the LEGISLATIVE authority of the nation in the matter of military establishments. That principle is unheard of except in one or two of our State constitutions, and all the rest reject it.

Suppose a stranger to our politics were to read our newspapers at the present moment without having examined the plan reported by the Convention. He would naturally be led to one of two conclusions: either that the plan contained a positive command that standing armies be kept up in time of peace, or that it gave the EXECUTIVE the whole power of levying troops, without making his discretion subject in any way to the control of the legislature.

If he then went on to read the plan itself, he would be surprised to find that neither was the case. He would find that the whole power of raising armies was placed in the LEGISLATURE, not in the EXECUTIVE; that this legislature was to be a popular body, made up of representatives of the people elected at regular intervals; and that, instead of the provision in favor of standing armies he had imagined, there was on this subject an important limit even on the legislature's discretion. This is the clause that forbids appropriating money for the support of an army for any longer period than two years. On a closer look, this precaution will prove to be a great and real security against keeping up troops without evident necessity.

Disappointed in his first guess, the person I have imagined would be inclined to carry his conjectures a little further. He would naturally say to himself that all this vehement and passionate declamation cannot be without some plausible pretext. It must be, he would reason, that this people, so jealous of their liberties, have inserted the most precise and rigid precautions on this point in all the earlier models of the constitutions they have established, and that the omission of these precautions from the new plan has given rise to all this alarm and clamor.

Suppose that, with this impression, he went on to review the individual State constitutions. How great would be his disappointment to find that TWO ONLY of them(1) contained a ban on standing armies in time of peace, and that the other eleven had either kept a profound silence on the subject or had expressly admitted the right of the Legislature to authorize their existence.

Still, he would be persuaded that there must be some plausible foundation for the cry raised on this subject. While any source of information remained unexplored, he could never imagine that it was nothing more than an experiment on the public's credulity, prompted either by a deliberate intention to deceive or by an excess of zeal too intemperate to be honest. It would probably occur to him that he might find the precautions he was looking for in the original compact between the States. Here, at last, he would expect to find the answer to the puzzle. No doubt, he would tell himself, the existing Confederation must contain the most explicit provisions against military establishments in time of peace, and a departure from this model on a favorite point has produced the discontent that seems to move these political champions.

Suppose he now applied himself to a careful and critical study of the Articles of Confederation. His astonishment would not only grow but would take on a touch of indignation, at the unexpected discovery that the Articles do not contain the prohibition he looked for. With jealous caution they had restricted the authority of the State legislatures in this respect, but they had not imposed a single restraint on that of the United States. If he happened to be a man of quick feeling or ardent temper, he could no longer refrain from regarding these clamors as the dishonest tricks of a sinister and unprincipled opposition to a plan that ought at least to receive a fair and open-minded examination from all sincere lovers of their country. How else, he would ask, could the authors of these clamors have been tempted to utter such loud censures on the plan about a point on which it seems to have conformed to the general sense of America, as declared in its different forms of government, and on which it has even added a new and powerful safeguard unknown to any of them? If, on the contrary, he happened to be a man of calm and dispassionate feelings, he would sigh over the frailty of human nature and lament that, in a matter so important to the happiness of millions, the true merits of the question should be confused and entangled by expedients so unfriendly to an impartial and correct judgment. Even such a man could hardly keep from remarking that conduct of this kind has too much the appearance of an intention to mislead the people by alarming their passions, rather than to convince them by arguments addressed to their understanding.

But however little this objection is supported even by precedents among ourselves, it may be worthwhile to take a closer look at its intrinsic merits. A close examination will show that restraints on the legislature's discretion over military establishments in time of peace would be improper to impose and, if imposed, would be unlikely to be observed, given the necessities of society.

Though a wide ocean separates the United States from Europe, there are various considerations that warn us against excessive confidence or security. On one side of us, stretching far to our rear, are growing settlements under the dominion of Britain. On the other side, extending to meet the British settlements, are colonies and establishments under the dominion of Spain. This situation, together with the nearness of the West India Islands belonging to these two powers, creates between them a common interest in regard to their American possessions and in relation to us. The savage tribes on our Western frontier ought to be regarded as our natural enemies and their natural allies, because they have most to fear from us and most to hope from them. Improvements in the art of navigation have, in making communication easier, made distant nations in great measure neighbors. Britain and Spain are among the principal maritime powers of Europe. A future agreement of aims between these nations ought not to be regarded as improbable. The growing distance of the blood relationship is every day weakening the force of the family compact between France and Spain, and politicians have always, with great reason, considered ties of blood to be feeble and uncertain links of political connection. Taken together, these circumstances warn us not to be too sanguine in thinking ourselves entirely out of the reach of danger.

Before the Revolution, and ever since the peace, there has been a constant necessity for keeping small garrisons on our Western frontier. No one can doubt that these will continue to be indispensable, if only against the ravages and plundering of the Indians. These garrisons must be supplied either by occasional detachments from the militia or by permanent corps in the pay of the government. The first is impracticable, and if it were practicable it would be harmful. The militia would not long submit, if at all, to being dragged from their occupations and families to perform that most disagreeable duty in times of profound peace. And if they could be persuaded or compelled to do it, the greater expense of frequent rotation of service, together with the loss of labor and the disruption of the productive pursuits of individuals, would be conclusive objections to the scheme. It would be as burdensome and injurious to the public as it would be ruinous to private citizens. The second resource, permanent corps in the pay of the government, amounts to a standing army in time of peace: a small one, indeed, but no less real for being small. Here is a simple view of the subject, and it shows us at once how improper a constitutional ban on such establishments would be, and how necessary it is to leave the matter to the discretion and prudence of the legislature.

As our strength increases, it is probable, indeed it may be said to be certain, that Britain and Spain will enlarge their military establishments in our neighborhood. If we are unwilling to be exposed, naked and defenseless, to their insults and encroachments, we shall find it advisable to increase our frontier garrisons in some proportion to the force that could harass our Western settlements. There are, and will be, particular posts whose possession will include command of large districts of territory and will make future invasions of the rest easier. It may be added that some of those posts will be keys to the trade with the Indian nations. Can anyone think it would be wise to leave such posts in a condition to be seized at any moment by one or the other of two neighboring and formidable powers? To act in that way would be to abandon all the usual maxims of prudence and policy.

If we mean to be a commercial people, or even to be secure on our Atlantic side, we must try to have a navy as soon as possible. For this purpose there must be dock-yards and arsenals, and for the defense of these, fortifications and probably garrisons. When a nation has become so powerful by sea that it can protect its dock-yards with its fleets, this removes the need for garrisons for that purpose. But where naval establishments are in their infancy, moderate garrisons will in all likelihood prove an indispensable security against landings aimed at destroying the arsenals and dock-yards, and sometimes the fleet itself.

1 This account of the matter is taken from the printed collection of State constitutions. Pennsylvania and North Carolina are the two that contain the ban, in these words: "As standing armies in time of peace are dangerous to liberty, THEY OUGHT NOT to be kept up." This is, in truth, rather a CAUTION than a PROHIBITION. New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Delaware, and Maryland have, in each of their bills of rights, a clause to this effect: "Standing armies are dangerous to liberty, and ought not to be raised or kept up WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF THE LEGISLATURE"; which is a formal admission of the authority of the Legislature. New York has no bill of rights, and her constitution says not a word about the matter. No bills of rights appear attached to the constitutions of the other States, except those just mentioned, and their constitutions are equally silent. I am told, however, that one or two States have bills of rights that do not appear in this collection, but that those also recognize the right of the legislative authority in this respect.
